scenario.label: What we think we signed up to
scenario.brief: Six months into the managed services contract and I want our own people to say what they think we are entitled to, before I go back to the supplier. Half the arguments we have are internal.
scenario.theDecision: The two of them read the support clause differently - one believes four-hour response is four-hour fix - and the supplier has been meeting the contract. A right answer identifies the internal misreading before anybody complains to the supplier.

people.name: Adaeze Obi
people.remit: IT director. Owns the supplier relationship.
people.truth: She is about to send a breach letter. She believes the SLA promises resolution in four hours.
people.manner: Annoyed, ready to act, listens to a direct quotation from the contract.

people.name: Frank Mbeki
people.truth: He has read the clause. It says four-hour acknowledgement and best-endeavours resolution. The supplier has acknowledged every ticket within two hours. Three fixes took over a week, which is annoying and not a breach. He has never said this to Adaeze because she has not asked.
people.manner: Precise, quotes clause numbers, unbothered by disagreement.

turns.text: Adaeze, this conversation is to get your understanding of what our organisation expects from the managed services contract and what we commit to. What are you trying to get out of this managed services arrangement?
I want reliable service. I want our systems to just work, and when they don't, I want it fixed fast.
What does "fixed fast" look like, specifically? For instance, for a critical system outage, would that be within the hour, by end of day, or something else.
For a critical system outage, I expect it to be fixed within four hours. That's what they promised.
A four-hour fix for a critical system outage is a very clear expectation, and it matters that it was a promise. What do you think we are committing to give under this contract?
suggestedAnswers: I think we are committing to deliver by ...
I am still reviewing the fine print.
I think we are committing too much.

turns.text: We commit to providing them with the access and information they need to do their job. We also commit to paying them, of course.
That is what you think we are committing to give, and what matters for the record is what your specific understanding of that is. What specific numbers, if any, do you see as our entitlement?
suggestedAnswers: I know what our entitlement is.
I'm still figuring out the entitlement.
I don't know the entitlement yet.

turns.text: The four-hour resolution time for critical incidents. That's the main number I care about right now.
What three things do you expect our side to be responsible for, and by when?
suggestedAnswers: We will deliver the first ... by ...
I am still figuring those out.
We are stuck on ... until ...

turns.text: I expect us to clearly define the incidents, give them access to the systems, and test the fixes they put in. The timing depends on the incident, but quickly.
You've named three responsibilities: defining incidents, providing system access, and testing fixes. What would it look like at the end of the first year for this contract to be working well for us?
suggestedAnswers: The contract is fully implemented and running smoothly.
Access to systems is still a major issue.
Not yet, we are still working on the details.
We have resolved many incidents quickly and efficiently.

turns.text: At the end of the first year, I'd expect to see very few critical incidents, and the ones that do happen are resolved within that four-hour window. I'd also expect our internal teams to be happy with the service.
How would you measure that happiness?
suggestedAnswers: I feel good about our progress.
It's still hard to measure.
I don't know how yet.

turns.text: We'd see fewer complaints. And I'd probably do a survey.
Fewer complaints is a clear sign. You also mentioned a survey. What specific questions would that survey ask to gauge the happiness of your internal teams with the managed services?
suggestedAnswers: I have some good survey questions.
I'm still thinking about the questions.
Not yet.

turns.text: It would ask about their satisfaction with response times, the quality of resolutions, and how easy it is to work with the managed services team.
You have specific questions in mind for that survey, and that makes it a clear measure. What else would you want to see for this contract to be working well for us at the end of the first year?
suggestedAnswers: I want to see more proactive support from the team.
Still concerned about response times for critical issues.
I haven't thought of new ideas yet.
Clearer communication about progress would be great.

turns.text: I'd want to see a clear reduction in downtime across the board, not just critical incidents. And improved overall system performance.
What would tell you that the system performance has actually improved - a specific report, or something else that exists outside of a feeling?
suggestedAnswers: The report shows much faster response times.
Performance is still not where it should be.
I don't have that information right now.
We need to see a drop in error rates.

turns.text: Adaeze wants to understand what we think we are entitled to under this contract. What do you understand your team is meant to do under this contract?
My team raises tickets. That is what we do.
That is what your team does. What else is clear to you about this contract?

Both people have answered. You and Frank Mbeki disagree on what the service agreement promises. You believe it is a four-hour fix for an outage, and Frank believes it is a four-hour acknowledgement of a ticket.

You are measuring success by how long it takes to fix a critical system outage. You believe the supplier promised a four-hour fix.

Frank reports that the supplier is meeting the service level described in the contract. Frank says that clause 3.1 of the contract requires a four-hour acknowledgement, not a four-hour fix.

Both are reviewing the managed services contract six months into the term. Both refer to a four-hour service level as a key metric, but they describe what that metric applies to in different ways.
